Jim Cramer Sticks With Palantir (PLTR) Despite Admitting His Target Was Too Aggressive
Jim Cramer maintained his bullish view of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) during Mad Money on October 1. Discussing its third-quarter stock performance, he commented:
On the first day of a brand new quarter, October 1, you need a compass. You know what provides you the best compass? What can navigate you the best? Last quarter… We all use S&P 500 as our benchmark in this business. Now, the index finished up 2.03% for the third quarter. Not bad, not great… Finally, there's Palantir, also up 60%. I believe in these guys. They're among the fastest growers with great gross margins and smart, tough leadership. I've been using a $250 price target. I've been too aggressive so far. The stock got as high as $207 and then it got walloped. It is now back to $190 where I would still buy Palantir.
Cramer recently likened Palantir to an NFL Wide Receiver ~a high-risk, high-reward growth stock that can deliver explosive upside.
Jim Cramer Sticks With Palantir (PLTR) Despite Admitting His Target Was Too Aggressive
Commercial AI Demand Extends The Expansion
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) reported second-quarter revenue of approximately $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year. U.S. commercial revenue increased 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue rose 90% to $809 million. The company generated $912 million in GAAP operating income, representing a 47% operating margin.
Following those results, management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion and its adjusted free cash flow outlook to $4.5 billion to $4.7 billion. The company also announced a partnership with Nebius on September 8 to give commercial customers access to additional AI computing infrastructure. Following integration, eligible customers will be able to use Nebius computing and inference services within Palantir's enterprise environment. The companies also plan to accelerate capacity deployment, including through modular data centers at locations with available power.

A Steep Multiple And Limits To Contract Visibility
Palantir Technologies Inc.'s (NASDAQ:PLTR) valuation remains a concern despite its rapid expansion. The company trades at approximately 100x forward earnings (depending on sources and different estimates), compared with <20x for the S&P 500.
Contract announcements also require careful interpretation. Palantir states that its total contract value and remaining deal value assume customers exercise their options and do not terminate agreements. Most contracts contain termination provisions, including termination for convenience, so these measures do not represent guaranteed future revenue. The company additionally identifies lengthy sales cycles and complex implementations as operating risks.
Michael Burry's criticism of the company also recently resurfaced.
Fund Participation Falls Despite The Rally
The number of hedge funds invested in Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) declined to 86 in Q2 from 96 in the previous quarter, according to Insider Monkey's tracking of more than 1,000 funds. Separately, short interest amounted to 2.80% of the public float as of mid-September.
Cramer remains willing to buy after the stock's pullback. Palantir's reported growth and profitability provide evidence for his enthusiasm, although the shares continue to command a considerable premium to the enterprise software comparison.

Though Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%) stock has pulled back somewhat, it has still delivered an incredible performance to investors, climbing more than 670% in five years. And over the past three months, the stock has gained fresh momentum, advancing 60%.
Investors have piled into Palantir stock as the company has shown itself to be an early winner in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Palantir offers its customers a way to easily and quickly harness the power of AI, and that's translated into tremendous demand and revenue growth.
The AI story continues, with key players such as chip designers and cloud service providers speaking of high demand, and that paints a bright future for Palantir. Could $20,000 invested in this tech company help you retire a millionaire? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
We'll start by considering the Palantir story so far. This company isn't new to the scene; it's actually been around for more than 20 years, and in its early days, mainly served government customers. Palantir develops software systems that gather a customer's data and put it to use. And a key moment took place a few years ago when Palantir released its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), a system that leverages the power of AI to analyze and use the data to make truly game-changing decisions.
Governments, particularly the U.S. government, have continued to appreciate Palantir's strengths, and this has kept government revenue climbing in the double digits. But the new element for Palantir has been the growth it's seen in its commercial business. The commercial customer has rushed to get in on AIP, and this has supercharged revenue growth in recent years.
The latest quarter is the perfect example. U.S. commercial revenue advanced 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue climbed 90% to $809 million. And total contract value (TCV) is on the rise too -- the company closed TCV of $3.3 billion, up 49% from the same period last year. U.S. commercial customer count has also skyrocketed from less than 20 just a few years ago to more than 600.

At the same time, Palantir hasn't been focused only on revenue. It's also done a fantastic job balancing growth with profitability, as we can see through its Rule of 40 score of 155%. A score of 40% is considered good, so clearly, Palantir is winning tremendously in this area.
Now, let's return to our question: As it's firing on all cylinders, can this AI player help you retire a millionaire?
We'll start by considering how a $20,000 investment in Palantir a few years ago would have played out. If you had invested that sum in the company a decade ago, today the value of your investment would be more than $390,000. That, along with investment in a variety of other quality stocks across industries, could have helped you along the path to millions.
Moving forward, Palantir could have room to run, particularly over the long term. Today, it trades for 116x forward earnings estimates, which isn't cheap, but it's important to keep in mind that the stock traded for more than 250x about a year ago. So investors will pay a premium for Palantir stock, suggesting that it could move higher from today's level.
It's also important to note that AI is just starting to be applied in the real world, so significant growth here may lie ahead. And Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count shows us two points that are very positive: Customer count is growing quickly, so momentum is there. But customer count still is low enough to offer considerable room for growth. All of this sets the stage for significant commercial revenue growth in the quarters and years to come.
Palantir, on its own, is unlikely to make you a millionaire. It's rare when one stock alone, even a top performer, will do the entire job, and it's too risky to bet on just one or two stocks to build wealth. But as part of a portfolio of quality stocks, this AI player could help you reach that goal as you retire.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) Stock: Partners With Armada on Sovereign AI Infrastructure
Palantir and Armada combine software and modular data centers for customer-owned sovereign AI deployments.
By Yasmin WernerOctober 2, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Palantir partners with Armada to expand sovereign AI infrastructure deployments.
Armada is named Palantir’s inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner.
Joint infrastructure keeps models, data, and hardware under customer control.
Modular data centers support faster deployment across secure operating sites.
Armada’s Sovereign AI Grid links distributed sites for stronger system resilience.
Palantir Technologies partnered with Armada to deliver sovereign artificial intelligence infrastructure for governments and enterprises. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) traded at $189.93, down 0.06%, after retreating from an intraday peak near $194.50. The companies will combine Palantir software with modular data centers manufactured in the United States and allied nations.
Palantir Names Armada Modular Data Center Partner
Palantir named Armada its inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner under the new agreement. The partnership combines Palantir’s Sovereign AI Operating System with Armada’s modular infrastructure and distributed network. Together, the companies aim to give customers direct ownership over computing systems, models, and stored data.
The offering targets organizations seeking infrastructure that operates within their own security boundaries. Therefore, customers can deploy open-weight models without depending on computing resources controlled by outside cloud providers. Armada also supports deployments at locations where existing power capacity can support new computing infrastructure.
Palantir will validate its operating system on Armada’s Galleon modular data centers. Its software stack includes AIP, Ontology, Foundry, and Apollo across the joint infrastructure. Meanwhile, Armada will provide the hardware, management software, and connectivity required across distributed deployments.
Partnership Extends Palantir Sovereign AI Architecture
The agreement expands Palantir’s existing Sovereign AI Operating System reference architecture developed with NVIDIA. That framework supports computing infrastructure that customers physically own and directly operate. The Armada partnership now brings that structure into modular data centers designed for faster deployment.
Customers can run open models and adapt them using proprietary company or government data. They can also serve those models through Palantir platforms without moving information outside controlled infrastructure. As a result, organizations can maintain direct authority over computing hardware and model operations.
Armada manufactures the modular data centers in the United States and selected allied nations. The companies designed the system for traditional sites, remote locations, and environments without standard network connections. The modular approach also reduces dependence on lengthy construction schedules for conventional data centers.
Armada Infrastructure Supports Distributed AI Deployments
Armada’s software platform manages open-source models for model tuning and inference across customer-owned infrastructure. The platform can function without Armada’s cloud services and supports fully air-gapped systems when required. It also monitors computing equipment, power systems, and cooling conditions across each deployment.
The Sovereign AI Grid connects individual locations into a broader distributed computing system. Organizations can spread important workloads across several sites instead of depending on one facility. This structure provides additional operational resilience when individual locations face outages or infrastructure problems.
Demand for locally controlled computing infrastructure has increased as organizations review cloud dependence and supply-chain exposure. Governments also seek stronger control over sensitive data, computing resources, and model deployment locations. Palantir and Armada now plan to address those requirements through an integrated customer-owned infrastructure stack.

Cash flow and compensation measure different things

This adjusted figure is neither GAAP free cash flow nor the exact amount required to offset dilution through repurchases. Stock awards are expensed according to accounting rules, while actual share issuance and the cash price of buybacks occur differently. The subtraction is useful as a sensitivity because compensation transfers part of the business's value to employees, even when it does not immediately consume cash.
The share count rose approximately 1.79% over the preceding year at the market-data snapshot. That is less dramatic than the growth in revenue, supporting the bullish argument that existing owners are still benefiting. Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom's custom AI chips are just getting started
Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure.
Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads.
The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips.
That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter.

The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years.
But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom.
Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation.
But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture.
Applied Digital is building the data centers powering AI
Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads.
It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion.
Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities.

That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models.
Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology.
Two different ways to invest beyond Palantir
For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks.
Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) investing is the most popular theme in the stock market right now. It's easy to understand why: Several companies are growing at incredible paces and could wind up being some of the major tech players of the future. Given how big a market opportunity AI has, there are several stocks that look like exciting investments investors should be buying right now.
Two of the most popular AI investments are Palantir (PLTR -0.68%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +7.36%). While SpaceX may not seem like a full-on AI investment, it acquired xAI, the maker of Grok, prior to its IPO, making it a major player in the AI arms race.
So, which of these two makes for the better buy? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
These two aren't necessarily competing against each other
Palantir and SpaceX are tackling similar but different segments of the AI market. Palantir's original product offering was suited for government use and found widespread adoption across many branches of government, both foreign and domestic. Eventually, its software was rolled out to the commercial sector, where it has likewise seen widespread adoption. Palantir's software is essentially a data analytics platform that utilizes AI to make sense of what it sees. It offers suggestions for the next action and either performs it itself or asks for human confirmation. Palantir's software works with pre-existing systems and can be successfully deployed in many different applications.

xAI from SpaceX is different. xAI has a family of large language models that can be deployed in many applications. But more importantly, applications can be built around its capabilities and utilized for different purposes.
Fundamentally, these are two different businesses. Palantir sells a ready-to-deploy software package, while xAI provides the building blocks for users to create their own or interact directly with it. These are both valid applications and have a massive market opportunity, but which one makes for the best investment opportunity?
Both stocks are expensive, but growing quickly
Last quarter, xAI's revenue grew by an impressive 213% year over year. However, SpaceX as a whole grew at a 92% pace -- still impressive, but slower.

Palantir's growth rate is right around SpaceX's total, increasing at a 93% year-over-year pace.
But SpaceX's AI division is growing at a quicker rate. Next year, Wall Street analysts estimate SpaceX's overall revenue will grow at a 153% year-over-year pace, with xAI likely leading the way. Wall Street expects Palantir to grow at a 50% rate next year, but it has downgraded Palantir's growth rate significantly over the past few years, so I'd take this projection with a grain of salt. However, I'd be surprised if SpaceX isn't growing faster than Palantir next year.
As for valuation, SpaceX currently trades for about 44 times this year's sales estimates. Palantir trades for 55 times this year's estimates.
Typically, a 20-times sales valuation is considered expensive, with 40 times sales being extremely expensive. That shows investors just how highly the market values these two stocks, and how high expectations are baked into them. As a result, investors must exercise some level of caution with these two, as there is a valuation risk associated with both stocks.
But which is the better buy? I think it's SpaceX. xAI's large language model approach will have more adoption than Palantir's turnkey AI solutions in the future, and that will drive further growth. With the company likely to grow at a faster pace and priced at a cheaper entry point, I think that also points to it being the better stock pick.

As the software market shifts toward products driven by artificial intelligence (AI), investors comparing enterprise software names may find themselves choosing between Salesforce (CRM -0.84%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%). This comparison looks at which company offers the better balance of value and growth.
Salesforce describes itself as a global leader in customer relationship management (CRM) technology and is now focused on Agentforce, its line of autonomous AI agents. Palantir sells software platforms that governments and companies use to integrate their data and apply AI to daily operations. For investors researching AI stocks to buy, the two companies present very different financial profiles.
Salesforce sells cloud-based software that helps businesses manage customer relationships and sales pipelines. Its annual report for fiscal 2026, which ended on Jan. 31, 2026, lists 83,334 employees and states that the company sells to businesses across almost every industry. On Aug. 26, 2026, Salesforce said annual recurring revenue from Agentforce had passed $1.5 billion. It completed its acquisition of Fin, an AI customer agent company formerly known as Intercom, on Sept. 10, 2026.
In fiscal 2026, revenue reached approximately $41.5 billion, up 9.6% from the prior fiscal year. Net income was nearly $7.5 billion, and net margin rose to 18% from 16.4%. About $1.0 billion in net gains from strategic investments contributed to that improvement, compared with a small net loss on those investments a year earlier.
As of Jan. 31, 2026, Salesforce had about $14.4 billion in total debt and $59.1 billion in shareholder equity, a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.2x. Its current ratio, which compares current assets with liabilities due within a year, was roughly 0.8x.
The debt picture has changed since then. Salesforce issued about $25 billion in debt in the quarter that ended April 30, 2026, to fund an accelerated share repurchase, and its July 31, 2026, balance sheet shows $39.3 billion in debt against $38.4 billion in equity, a ratio of about 1.0x.
Free cash flow, defined as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, was about $14.4 billion in fiscal 2026. Stock-based compensation (SBC) equaled roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which is worth noting because SBC is a non-cash expense that is added back in the cash flow statement.
Palantir develops software platforms that help organizations integrate their data and operations, and it sells them to government agencies and commercial customers.
Government customers supplied 54% of its 2025 revenue. Palantir also works with other companies that investors follow as tech stocks, including a collaboration with Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%) announced on Sept. 10, 2026, and a global partnership with Fujitsu (FJTSF +0.97%). Its commercial customer count reached 870 for the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, up 26% from a year earlier.
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached roughly $4.5 billion, a 56.2% year-over-year increase. Palantir reported net income of about $1.6 billion. Net margin was about 36.3%, up from 16.1% in 2024.
Palantir had no debt outstanding as of Dec. 31, 2025, resulting in a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x. Its current ratio at that date was approximately 7.1x, indicating ample liquid assets to cover short-term liabilities. Free cash flow, calculated the same way as for Salesforce (operating cash flow minus capital expenditures), was about $2.1 billion.
Palantir's own adjusted free cash flow, which adds back employer payroll taxes tied to stock-based compensation, was about $2.3 billion. SBC equaled roughly 32% of operating cash flow.
Salesforce competes with established enterprise software vendors and AI-native start-ups in a market that its annual report calls highly competitive. Salesforce and its Slack unit sued Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) in London's High Court in April 2026, alleging that the tying and bundling of Teams harmed competition.
Microsoft has said the case lacks merit, and the outcome is uncertain. Salesforce must also integrate large acquisitions such as Informatica, which closed in fiscal 2026, and Fin, and it now carries far more debt than it did at the start of the fiscal year. On Sept. 29, 2026, it also agreed to acquire Listen Labs, an AI customer research company, in a deal it expects to close in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.
Palantir's annual report flags a limited number of customers that account for a substantial portion of its revenue, with the top three supplying 16% of 2025 revenue, and a sales cycle it calls long and unpredictable.
The company depends on third-party computing infrastructure. It also warns that news coverage or other outside scrutiny of the company or its leadership could harm its reputation. A shareholder lawsuit that a federal court dismissed in April 2025 was still on appeal as of June 30, 2026.
Salesforce trades at a much lower forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, and a much lower P/S ratio, which measures price relative to sales over the past 12 months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Salesforce looks like the better buy to me, with the caveat that it's a slower-growing and more indebted company than the fiscal 2026 figures above suggest. On Aug. 26, 2026, management guided for revenue growth of 11% to 12% in fiscal 2027, which ends in January 2027.
By its own math, more than a quarter of that growth comes from the Informatica acquisition. Salesforce also borrowed heavily earlier this year to fund its accelerated share repurchase. Its debt has more than doubled since January and roughly equaled shareholder equity at the end of July. The appeal is the price.
A business that turns about a third of its revenue into free cash flow, at a forward P/E in the mid-teens, leaves room for Agentforce to grow slowly without the investment case falling apart.
Palantir is growing far faster. Its revenue nearly doubled in the second quarter, and on Aug. 3, 2026, management raised its full-year outlook. The catch is a forward P/E ratio more than five times Salesforce's, which leaves the stock with little cushion if growth cools.
Growth rates this high are also hard to sustain as a company gets bigger. I'd rather hold Palantir as a small position in a diversified portfolio than pay that premium for a large one. Even so, a company expanding this quickly with no debt has earned a spot on a growth investor's watch list.

Jim Cramer maintained his bullish view of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) during Mad Money on October 1. Discussing its third-quarter stock performance, he commented:
On the first day of a brand new quarter, October 1, you need a compass. You know what provides you the best compass? What can navigate you the best? Last quarter… We all use S&P 500 as our benchmark in this business. Now, the index finished up 2.03% for the third quarter. Not bad, not great… Finally, there's Palantir, also up 60%. I believe in these guys. They're among the fastest growers with great gross margins and smart, tough leadership. I've been using a $250 price target. I've been too aggressive so far. The stock got as high as $207 and then it got walloped. It is now back to $190 where I would still buy Palantir.
Cramer recently likened Palantir to an NFL Wide Receiver ~a high-risk, high-reward growth stock that can deliver explosive upside.

Commercial AI Demand Extends The Expansion
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) reported second-quarter revenue of approximately $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year. U.S. commercial revenue increased 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue rose 90% to $809 million. The company generated $912 million in GAAP operating income, representing a 47% operating margin.
Following those results, management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion and its adjusted free cash flow outlook to $4.5 billion to $4.7 billion. The company also announced a partnership with Nebius on September 8 to give commercial customers access to additional AI computing infrastructure. Following integration, eligible customers will be able to use Nebius computing and inference services within Palantir's enterprise environment. The companies also plan to accelerate capacity deployment, including through modular data centers at locations with available power.

A Steep Multiple And Limits To Contract Visibility
Palantir Technologies Inc.'s (NASDAQ:PLTR) valuation remains a concern despite its rapid expansion. The company trades at approximately 100x forward earnings (depending on sources and different estimates), compared with <20x for the S&P 500.
Contract announcements also require careful interpretation. Palantir states that its total contract value and remaining deal value assume customers exercise their options and do not terminate agreements. Most contracts contain termination provisions, including termination for convenience, so these measures do not represent guaranteed future revenue. The company additionally identifies lengthy sales cycles and complex implementations as operating risks.
Michael Burry's criticism of the company also recently resurfaced.
Fund Participation Falls Despite The Rally
The number of hedge funds invested in Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) declined to 86 in Q2 from 96 in the previous quarter, according to Insider Monkey's tracking of more than 1,000 funds. Separately, short interest amounted to 2.80% of the public float as of mid-September.
Cramer remains willing to buy after the stock's pullback. Palantir's reported growth and profitability provide evidence for his enthusiasm, although the shares continue to command a considerable premium to the enterprise software comparison.
While we acknowledge the potential of PLTR as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Though Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%) stock has pulled back somewhat, it has still delivered an incredible performance to investors, climbing more than 670% in five years. And over the past three months, the stock has gained fresh momentum, advancing 60%.
Investors have piled into Palantir stock as the company has shown itself to be an early winner in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Palantir offers its customers a way to easily and quickly harness the power of AI, and that's translated into tremendous demand and revenue growth.
The AI story continues, with key players such as chip designers and cloud service providers speaking of high demand, and that paints a bright future for Palantir. Could $20,000 invested in this tech company help you retire a millionaire? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
We'll start by considering the Palantir story so far. This company isn't new to the scene; it's actually been around for more than 20 years, and in its early days, mainly served government customers. Palantir develops software systems that gather a customer's data and put it to use. And a key moment took place a few years ago when Palantir released its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), a system that leverages the power of AI to analyze and use the data to make truly game-changing decisions.
Governments, particularly the U.S. government, have continued to appreciate Palantir's strengths, and this has kept government revenue climbing in the double digits. But the new element for Palantir has been the growth it's seen in its commercial business. The commercial customer has rushed to get in on AIP, and this has supercharged revenue growth in recent years.
The latest quarter is the perfect example. U.S. commercial revenue advanced 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue climbed 90% to $809 million. And total contract value (TCV) is on the rise too -- the company closed TCV of $3.3 billion, up 49% from the same period last year. U.S. commercial customer count has also skyrocketed from less than 20 just a few years ago to more than 600.

At the same time, Palantir hasn't been focused only on revenue. It's also done a fantastic job balancing growth with profitability, as we can see through its Rule of 40 score of 155%. A score of 40% is considered good, so clearly, Palantir is winning tremendously in this area.
Now, let's return to our question: As it's firing on all cylinders, can this AI player help you retire a millionaire?
We'll start by considering how a $20,000 investment in Palantir a few years ago would have played out. If you had invested that sum in the company a decade ago, today the value of your investment would be more than $390,000. That, along with investment in a variety of other quality stocks across industries, could have helped you along the path to millions.
Moving forward, Palantir could have room to run, particularly over the long term. Today, it trades for 116x forward earnings estimates, which isn't cheap, but it's important to keep in mind that the stock traded for more than 250x about a year ago. So investors will pay a premium for Palantir stock, suggesting that it could move higher from today's level.
It's also important to note that AI is just starting to be applied in the real world, so significant growth here may lie ahead. And Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count shows us two points that are very positive: Customer count is growing quickly, so momentum is there. But customer count still is low enough to offer considerable room for growth. All of this sets the stage for significant commercial revenue growth in the quarters and years to come.
Palantir, on its own, is unlikely to make you a millionaire. It's rare when one stock alone, even a top performer, will do the entire job, and it's too risky to bet on just one or two stocks to build wealth. But as part of a portfolio of quality stocks, this AI player could help you reach that goal as you retire.

Why Palantir Could Be One of the Decade’s Biggest Growth Stocks
Palantir just posted numbers that left Wall Street scrambling to justify its own cautious price targets, and the real question is whether the valuation ceiling everyone keeps citing is about to become a floor.
Published October 2, 2026, 10:00am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR | PLTR Price Prediction) is $202.08 over the next 12 months. That implies 8.08% upside from the model’s $186.97 starting price. Our model gives the stock a high-confidence buy rating.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Palantir posted the fastest revenue growth in its history and raised full-year guidance for the second straight quarter. The upside in our target is modest because the valuation already reflects much of that momentum. The growth path is long enough that Palantir can keep compounding well past our 12-month window.
A 93% Growth Quarter Restarted Palantir’s Rally
Shares rose 2.36% over the past week and are up 6.53% year to date at $189.36 this morning. The stock is 8.8% below its $207.52 52-week high and 78% above its $106.37 low.
Revenue grew 92.83% to $1.935 billion. EPS came in at $0.41 against a $0.28 estimate, which made it the ninth consecutive beat. Full-year revenue guidance now is at $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion, up from the $7.182 billion to $7.198 billion range Palantir gave in February. PwC also expanded its strategic alliance with Palantir on September 3 to help organizations scale enterprise AI.
Net dollar retention reached 157%, and total remaining deal value hit $13.1 billion, up 83%. Palantir closed 73 deals worth $10 million or more in the quarter. CEO Alex Karp said, “I am driving the business to grow at a rate equal to or above what we have in U.S. commercial for the next 18 months.”
The adjusted operating margin reached 62%, and Palantir guides for $4.50 billion to $4.70 billion in adjusted free cash flow for the year. 21 analysts rate the stock a buy or strong buy. Under the most optimistic scenario, shares reach $219.27.
Valuation and Dilution Could Cap the Upside
Shares trade at 159x trailing earnings and 85x forward earnings. Stock-based compensation was $265 million in Q2, and gains on Palantir’s SpaceX stake added $0.03 to GAAP EPS. Government contracts terminable for convenience pose a risk.
Two analysts rate the stock a sell or strong sell, and the downside scenario points to $170.18. Q2 free cash flow of $1.220 billion far exceeded stock-based compensation, while adjusted expenses rose 37% due to AI platform investment and technical hiring.
How Palantir Stacks Up Against Snowflake and MongoDB
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) competes for enterprise AI data budgets with 35.09% revenue growth but a GAAP operating loss of $263 million.
MongoDB (NASDAQ:MDB) sells AI-ready databases with 30.5% revenue growth.
Palantir is growing close to three times as fast as either peer and at far higher margins. Against that group, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable, and arguably conservative.
Palantir’s Growth Tips the Scale Toward Our Buy Rating
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $202.08 carries a buy rating and 90% confidence. What tips the scale is Palantir’s ability to keep speeding up growth while margins expand.
I would view shares more favorably if U.S. commercial growth holds above 100% into 2027. I would grow more cautious if the pace of deal closings slows while the stock still trades at 85x forward earnings.
Palantir’s profile, hypergrowth at scale with expanding margins, mirrors the early traits of past tech giants. We collected those signs in a free playbook you can grab here.

Jim Cramer maintained his bullish view of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) during Mad Money on October 1. Discussing its third-quarter stock performance, he commented:
On the first day of a brand new quarter, October 1, you need a compass. You know what provides you the best compass? What can navigate you the best? Last quarter… We all use S&P 500 as our benchmark in this business. Now, the index finished up 2.03% for the third quarter. Not bad, not great… Finally, there’s Palantir, also up 60%. I believe in these guys. They’re among the fastest growers with great gross margins and smart, tough leadership. I’ve been using a $250 price target. I’ve been too aggressive so far. The stock got as high as $207 and then it got walloped. It is now back to $190 where I would still buy Palantir.
Cramer recently likened Palantir to an NFL Wide Receiver ~a high-risk, high-reward growth stock that can deliver explosive upside.
Commercial AI Demand Extends The Expansion
Palantir Technologies Inc. reported second-quarter revenue of approximately $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year. U.S. commercial revenue increased 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue rose 90% to $809 million. The company generated $912 million in GAAP operating income, representing a 47% operating margin.
Following those results, management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion and its adjusted free cash flow outlook to $4.5 billion to $4.7 billion. The company also announced a partnership with Nebius on September 8 to give commercial customers access to additional AI computing infrastructure. Following integration, eligible customers will be able to use Nebius computing and inference services within Palantir’s enterprise environment. The companies also plan to accelerate capacity deployment, including through modular data centers at locations with available power.
Don’t Miss: Jim Cramer Explains Why Palantir’s Rule of 40 Dominance Proves Bears Wrong
A Steep Multiple And Limits To Contract Visibility
Palantir Technologies Inc.’s valuation remains a concern despite its rapid expansion. The company trades at approximately 100x forward earnings (depending on sources and different estimates), compared with <20x for the S&P 500.
Contract announcements also require careful interpretation. Palantir states that its total contract value and remaining deal value assume customers exercise their options and do not terminate agreements. Most contracts contain termination provisions, including termination for convenience, so these measures do not represent guaranteed future revenue. The company additionally identifies lengthy sales cycles and complex implementations as operating risks.
Michael Burry’s criticism of the company also recently resurfaced.
Fund Participation Falls Despite The Rally
The number of hedge funds invested in Palantir Technologies Inc. declined to 86 in Q2 from 96 in the previous quarter, according to Insider Monkey’s tracking of more than 1,000 funds. Separately, short interest amounted to 2.80% of the public float as of mid-September.
Cramer remains willing to buy after the stock’s pullback. Palantir’s reported growth and profitability provide evidence for his enthusiasm, although the shares continue to command a considerable premium to the enterprise software comparison.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) Stock: Partners With Armada on Sovereign AI Infrastructure
Palantir and Armada combine software and modular data centers for customer-owned sovereign AI deployments.
By Yasmin WernerOctober 2, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Palantir partners with Armada to expand sovereign AI infrastructure deployments.
Armada is named Palantir’s inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner.
Joint infrastructure keeps models, data, and hardware under customer control.
Modular data centers support faster deployment across secure operating sites.
Armada’s Sovereign AI Grid links distributed sites for stronger system resilience.
Palantir Technologies partnered with Armada to deliver sovereign artificial intelligence infrastructure for governments and enterprises. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) traded at $189.93, down 0.06%, after retreating from an intraday peak near $194.50. The companies will combine Palantir software with modular data centers manufactured in the United States and allied nations.
Palantir Names Armada Modular Data Center Partner
Palantir named Armada its inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner under the new agreement. The partnership combines Palantir’s Sovereign AI Operating System with Armada’s modular infrastructure and distributed network. Together, the companies aim to give customers direct ownership over computing systems, models, and stored data.
The offering targets organizations seeking infrastructure that operates within their own security boundaries. Therefore, customers can deploy open-weight models without depending on computing resources controlled by outside cloud providers. Armada also supports deployments at locations where existing power capacity can support new computing infrastructure.
Palantir will validate its operating system on Armada’s Galleon modular data centers. Its software stack includes AIP, Ontology, Foundry, and Apollo across the joint infrastructure. Meanwhile, Armada will provide the hardware, management software, and connectivity required across distributed deployments.
Partnership Extends Palantir Sovereign AI Architecture
The agreement expands Palantir’s existing Sovereign AI Operating System reference architecture developed with NVIDIA. That framework supports computing infrastructure that customers physically own and directly operate. The Armada partnership now brings that structure into modular data centers designed for faster deployment.
Customers can run open models and adapt them using proprietary company or government data. They can also serve those models through Palantir platforms without moving information outside controlled infrastructure. As a result, organizations can maintain direct authority over computing hardware and model operations.
Armada manufactures the modular data centers in the United States and selected allied nations. The companies designed the system for traditional sites, remote locations, and environments without standard network connections. The modular approach also reduces dependence on lengthy construction schedules for conventional data centers.
Armada Infrastructure Supports Distributed AI Deployments
Armada’s software platform manages open-source models for model tuning and inference across customer-owned infrastructure. The platform can function without Armada’s cloud services and supports fully air-gapped systems when required. It also monitors computing equipment, power systems, and cooling conditions across each deployment.
The Sovereign AI Grid connects individual locations into a broader distributed computing system. Organizations can spread important workloads across several sites instead of depending on one facility. This structure provides additional operational resilience when individual locations face outages or infrastructure problems.
Demand for locally controlled computing infrastructure has increased as organizations review cloud dependence and supply-chain exposure. Governments also seek stronger control over sensitive data, computing resources, and model deployment locations. Palantir and Armada now plan to address those requirements through an integrated customer-owned infrastructure stack.

Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR)
, a constituent of the Nasdaq Composite, the S&P 500 and the [Nasdaq-100], is in focus in today's Technical Analysis coverage today. Palantir Technologies is a data analytics and AI software company serving governments and commercial customers. The stock is drawing attention as Wall Street weighs AI momentum, shifting oil prices and bond yields, with investors looking closely at how individual companies are positioned for a more selective market.
Market participants are balancing several competing forces in the current session. On one side, AI-related spending continues to support parts of the technology complex. On the other, fluctuating oil prices, elevated bond yields and uncertainty about the path of monetary policy have kept investors cautious. Breadth has been uneven, with leadership concentrated in a limited number of sectors, and that has encouraged a more selective approach to stock picking across the market.
Palantir Technologies develops software platforms, including Gotham for government and defence, Foundry for commercial organisations and its Artificial Intelligence Platform, known as AIP. Its software helps organisations integrate data and deploy AI in operations. US commercial revenue has grown quickly as businesses adopt AIP, while government contracts remain a major source of revenue.
From a technical perspective, Palantir has seen strong momentum and high volatility. Traders watch trading volume, moving averages and relative strength, while fundamentals such as revenue growth and contract wins influence long-term trends.
Technical analysis focuses on price trends, trading volume and chart patterns rather than company fundamentals. Traders commonly watch moving averages, such as the 50-day and 200-day lines, as well as momentum indicators like the relative strength index and levels of support and resistance. Highly traded, volatile stocks tend to attract technical traders because sharp moves can create short-term opportunities. However, technical signals work best when combined with an understanding of the fundamental and market factors driving a stock.
Technical traders commonly look at whether a stock is trading above or below its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, with crosses between the two often seen as signals of trend changes. The relative strength index helps identify overbought or oversold conditions, while volume can confirm the strength of a move. Support and resistance levels, based on past price action, are used to set entry and exit points. Traders also watch options activity and short interest in highly traded stocks.
Beyond company-specific developments, Palantir Technologies is also influenced by the wider economic backdrop. Inflation trends and Federal Reserve expectations shape interest rates, which in turn affect financing conditions and valuations. Energy prices influence costs for businesses and households, while trade policy and tariffs have become an important variable for many companies with global supply chains. The strength of AI-related investment continues to shape sentiment across much of the market.
Palantir's AIP platform lets customers build AI applications that connect to their data and operations, and the company runs 'bootcamps' to help customers deploy it quickly. Government customers include the US Department of Defense and intelligence agencies, as well as governments in Europe. Palantir's Maven Smart System contract with the Army is among its largest. The company has reported rapid revenue growth and expanding profit margins.
Readers can track revenue growth, US commercial customer count, government contracts, trading volume and key moving averages.
How Palantir Technologies fits the Technical Analysis theme
Within Technical Analysis, Palantir Technologies offers a useful example of how company-specific factors interact with sector-wide trends. When the group moves together, broad themes such as interest rates or commodity prices are usually the driver. When Palantir Technologies diverges from peers, the explanation is more likely to be found in its own operating results, strategic decisions or news flow. Watching how the stock behaves relative to its sector can therefore provide insight into how the market views its individual prospects.
Investor sentiment toward Palantir Technologies can change quickly as new information emerges. Earnings reports, management commentary, analyst updates and industry news all play a role. In the current environment, where sector leadership is narrow and macro signals are mixed, the market has tended to reward companies that show clear evidence of demand and disciplined execution, while punishing those that disappoint on growth or margins.
As with any listed company, Palantir Technologies faces risks that could affect its performance. These include changes in demand for its products or services, competitive pressure, regulatory and policy developments, and shifts in the broader economic environment. Execution on strategic priorities and the ability to manage costs in an uncertain market will also influence results. Readers following the stock should weigh both the opportunities and the challenges described above.
The current attention on Palantir Technologies reflects both its own business developments and the broader forces shaping Technical Analysis. With markets rewarding selectivity, the company's execution and the direction of macro factors such as yields and energy prices will likely remain central to how the stock is viewed.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) received a higher Wall Street price target after DA Davidson reaffirmed its bullish stance on the software and artificial intelligence company.
In a research note published on September 11, analyst Gil Luria maintained a ‘Buy’ rating on Palantir stock and raised the firm’s price target to $250 from $200.
According to the note, customer interest in AI sovereignty continues to strengthen Palantir’s position in the enterprise AI market.
The analyst highlighted the company’s ability to act as a control plane and orchestration layer that helps organizations manage multiple AI models while controlling costs.
DA Davidson also pointed to the technology company’s expanding role in helping customers choose, deploy, and manage AI systems across different providers.
The firm believes this approach is resonating with enterprises seeking greater flexibility rather than relying on a single AI vendor.
The higher valuation target was also supported by broader strength across software stocks and confidence in Palantir’s long-term growth trajectory.
The latest DA Davidson target places the analyst among the most bullish voices on Wall Street. According to analyst consensus data from TipRanks, 23 analysts currently cover Palantir stock, with an average 12-month price target of $200.53 and a high target of $255.
PLTR 12-month stock price chart. Source: TipRanks
The analyst upgrade follows a strong second-quarter performance from Palantir. The company reported revenue of $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year, while adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.41, ahead of Wall Street expectations.
Growth was particularly strong in the U.S. commercial segment, where revenue surged 149% to $764 million. U.S. government revenue also posted growth of about 90%.
Following the earnings report, Palantir raised its full-year 2026 guidance. The company now expects revenue of approximately $8.15 billion, representing annual growth of more than 80%, while projecting adjusted free cash flow of between $4.5 billion and $4.7 billion.
Recent developments have also strengthened Palantir’s AI strategy, with the company having expanded its partnership with Nvidia by integrating Nemotron open models into Foundry and its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), supporting sovereign AI deployments for sensitive industries and supply chains.
While many analysts remain optimistic about Palantir’s AI-driven growth, strong profitability, and expanding commercial business, valuation continues to be a key point of debate.
The stock trades at premium multiples compared to most software peers, leaving investors closely watching whether the company’s rapid growth can continue at its current pace.

Is Palantir’s Cash Flow Keeping Ahead of Share Dilution?
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) is producing substantially more cash as its revenue expands. The investment question is whether that growth is large enough, per share, to compensate for stock compensation and the price investors are paying. A rising company-wide cash balance can coexist with a demanding shareholder valuation.
At September 30, Palantir's market capitalization was approximately $449.49 billion. The stock traded at roughly 134 times trailing free cash flow. Strong business execution is therefore necessary but may still be insufficient if much of its benefit is already capitalized in the share price.
Is Palantir's Cash Flow Keeping Ahead of Share Dilution?
Fast-growing enterprise software carries very different prices. Our Palantir-versus-Snowflake analysis asks whether Palantir or Snowflake better justifies its valuation, with ownership costs helping determine the answer.
Cash flow and compensation measure different things
First-half operating cash flow was $2.115 billion and capital expenditure $21.96 million, producing about $2.093 billion of simple free cash flow. First-half stock-based compensation was $466.8 million. Subtracting that compensation produces an illustrative $1.627 billion owner-cost proxy, roughly 22% below reported free cash flow.
This adjusted figure is neither GAAP free cash flow nor the exact amount required to offset dilution through repurchases. Stock awards are expensed according to accounting rules, while actual share issuance and the cash price of buybacks occur differently. The subtraction is useful as a sensitivity because compensation transfers part of the business's value to employees, even when it does not immediately consume cash.
The share count rose approximately 1.79% over the preceding year at the market-data snapshot. That is less dramatic than the growth in revenue, supporting the bullish argument that existing owners are still benefiting. It also means a company-wide growth rate should not be presented as an identical per-share growth rate.
Valuation raises the required performance
Short interest was 60,184,903 shares at the September 15 settlement, about 2.8% of float, with 2.24 days to cover. The valuation question remains about future cash per share, regardless of that dated positioning.
Annualizing the first-half free cash flow produces about $4.19 billion. At the current market capitalization, that illustrative pace implies around 107 times cash flow. Annualizing the owner-cost proxy gives $3.25 billion and a multiple near 138. The figures are not forecasts and do not replace a full-year model; they show how the compensation assumption changes valuation on the same period basis.
To bring the equity value down to 40 times sustainable annual free cash flow would require roughly $11.24 billion of annual cash generation. That is about 2.7 times the annualized first-half figure before any compensation adjustment. At 30 times, the required annual amount rises to nearly $15 billion. A high price requires a larger future business even when current margins are strong.
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database showed 86 Palantir holders in Q2 2026, down from 96 in Q1. Arrowstreet nevertheless increased its common-share position 97% to 20,517,115 shares. These positions precede the August 3 results and demonstrate that broader participation and individual fund sizing can move in opposite directions.
Palantir's second-quarter revenue grew 93% to $1.94 billion, with US commercial sales up 149% to $764 million. GAAP operating income reached $912 million, while adjusted operating income was $1.19 billion. Those results give the bullish case substance: rapid growth is arriving with meaningful operating profit rather than only an adjusted promise of future scale.
The bearish case concerns duration and ownership economics. Growth may slow before the cash-flow level implied by the price is reached, or compensation and reinvestment may absorb more of the incremental profit than expected. Even continued business growth can produce a poor stock return if investors ultimately pay a lower multiple for it.
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) is growing cash earnings fast enough to make the business case credible. Its starting valuation still demands much more growth per diluted share. Strong conversion and restrained ownership costs would support that requirement; slower growth or heavier compensation would leave less room for an ordinary result.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of PLTR as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. If you are looking for an AI stock that is more promising than PLTR and that has 10,000% upside potential, check out our report about this cheapest AI stock.

Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom (AVGO +3.35%) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), while Applied Digital (APLD +5.05%) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look.
Image source: Getty Images.
Broadcom's custom AI chips are just getting started
Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure.
Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads.
The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips.
That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter.
$1.7TMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years.
But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom.
Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation.
But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture.
Applied Digital is building the data centers powering AI
Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads.
It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion.
Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. Its Polaris Forge 1 campus in North Dakota has already kicked off operations, and additional capacity will keep coming online as construction continues. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities.
$7.6BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Another important development was its move to hive off its cloud services business into a new public company, ChronoScale (CHRN -0.83%). This will allow Applied Digital to focus more on developing and running large-scale AI campuses. That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models.
Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology.
Two different ways to invest beyond Palantir
For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks.
Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI.
Which one is the better choice for your portfolio likely depends on how much risk you're willing to take on.

A Second-Quarter Earnings Beat Sparked a Sharp Rebound
Palantir traded near $123.06 on August 1. A week later it was at $172.01, after the August 3 earnings report. Shares are up 6.2% year to date and 1.28% over the past month, but down 1.57% this week. The stock sits 9% below its 52-week high of $207.52 and 77% higher than its low of $106.37.
Second-quarter EPS of $0.41 exceeded the $0.28 estimate, Palantir’s ninth consecutive beat. Revenue reached $1.935 billion, up 92.83%. U.S. commercial revenue grew 149% to $764 million. CEO Alex Karp called the quarter “otherworldly,” pointing to a Rule of 40 score of 155%.

The 2027 EPS consensus has risen to $2.3267 from $2.0821 90 days ago, with 26 upward revisions and zero cuts in 30 days. If AI sovereignty demand speeds up, the bull case reaches $219.29.
A Premium Valuation Leaves Little Room for a Stumble
Palantir trades at 160x trailing earnings and 73x sales. Its government contracts can be ended for convenience, and stock-based compensation reached $265 million last quarter. Our bear case is $170.22. Even so, GAAP operating margin reached 47% after those compensation costs, so profitability already covers the dilution.
Palantir Outgrows CrowdStrike, Snowflake and ServiceNow
CrowdStrike (NASDAQ:CRWD) is in the same software-infrastructure industry and also carries a premium for AI exposure. The stock changes hands at 208x forward earnings on 25.8% revenue growth.
Also competing with Palantir for enterprise data and AI workloads is Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW), yet its 169x forward multiple comes with 35.1% growth.
ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) is the value contrast, trading at 28x forward earnings on 24% growth.
Palantir is growing several times faster than its high-multiple peers and trades at a lower forward multiple than both. Measured against that group, our 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable and even conservative.
Palantir Earns Its Premium, and the Upside Is Still Building
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $202.14 comes with a buy rating and 90% confidence. What tips the scale is the steady stream of upward earnings revisions.
The case gets stronger if U.S. commercial growth stays above 100% and the third quarter beats the $2.160 billion to $2.164 billion revenue guide. It weakens if deal momentum slows while the multiple stays extended. For now, growth is exceeding the valuation.
Looking further ahead, here is where our model projects Palantir could trade at each year’s end, assuming current growth trends and market conditions hold.

Attention across U.S. markets has shifted back toward company execution after a volatile macro backdrop involving interest rates, energy costs and technology-led market leadership. For readers following the AI Stocks space, the key question is how business fundamentals and sector conditions interact as the market digests fresh policy and industry signals. , remains closely tied to these operating considerations.
Behind Today's Added Curiosity?
The current market backdrop matters because enterprise AI deployment and software adoption is tied to decisions that can influence demand, procurement, customer budgets and management priorities. Palantir Technologies Inc. operates in an environment where these factors can change quickly, so the quality of execution is likely to matter more than broad market enthusiasm. That broader setting can be read alongside the Nasdaq Composite benchmark, which provides context for the companys position in the U.S. equity market. The latest U.S. market cycle has shown that sector leadership can rotate sharply when bond yields, energy prices or policy expectations move, which puts additional emphasis on company-specific delivery.
For Palantir Technologies Inc., today's discussion can be framed around whether its existing strategy matches the direction of its industry. This places the company within the broader AI Stocks landscape, where peer trends can add context to its company-specific developments. A business can benefit from a supportive sector trend only when it has the capacity, product relevance, commercial relationships and operating discipline needed to convert that trend into durable activity. That makes execution, rather than market mood, the central lens for interpreting the company within AI Stocks.
The company also sits within a market that is paying closer attention to the relationship between growth ambitions and funding conditions. Even firms with attractive end markets may face a higher bar when capital is more expensive or customers become more selective. In that setting, management clarity, project sequencing and customer concentration become important indicators of how well a business can adapt.
How Sector-Wide Cycles Tie In Here?
The latest U.S. session has been influenced by a combination of monetary-policy expectations, easing oil pressure and renewed appetite for technology-linked themes. These forces do not affect every company in the same way, but they can change discount rates, procurement decisions and risk tolerance across the economy. For a AI Stocks name such as Palantir Technologies Inc., the key is to separate broad market movement from changes that genuinely affect the operating model.
Easing energy costs can relieve input pressure across the economy, while movement in bond yields alters financing conditions for companies and customers alike. At the same time, renewed focus on artificial-intelligence infrastructure keeps pulling capital toward data centres, power demand, networking, semiconductors and connected supply chains. Businesses outside technology can still be shaped by shifts in electricity demand, construction activity, logistics or consumer spending.
This cross-sector backdrop means company analysis needs to stay grounded in operating exposure. Palantir Technologies Inc. may be influenced by the same macro themes as its peers, but the magnitude depends on customer mix, cost structure, regulatory requirements and the timing of strategic programs. That is why the current session is best used as context rather than as a substitute for company-level assessment.
Why Demand Quality Merit A Look?
One important lens here is the durability of demand. For Palantir Technologies Inc., demand is more informative when it is supported by repeat customers, long-duration contracts, recurring usage or clearly defined end-market needs. A headline-driven surge in interest can fade quickly, whereas sustained customer activity tends to provide a better foundation for planning capacity, staffing and capital allocation. Beyond the headline figures, the pattern of repeat activity often says more than a single strong period, since durable demand tends to hold up across multiple cycles rather than fading once initial attention moves elsewhere. A useful check is whether demand is broadening across customer groups or concentrated in a narrow segment, since broader participation generally signals a healthier underlying trend than a single pocket of strength.
How Delivery Focus Shapes Results?
A further consideration is how well execution holds up. Management teams across AI Stocks are being asked to balance growth initiatives with cost discipline, supply-chain reliability and changing financing conditions. For Palantir Technologies Inc., that balance may show up through project timing, product launches, manufacturing utilization, commercial partnerships or service delivery. Slippage in one area can affect the rest of the operating plan, while steady execution can improve visibility. Consistency across several reporting periods tends to matter more than any single strong stretch, since steady delivery builds the kind of track record that supports confidence during less favourable conditions.
Why Long-Term Logic Remains Key?
A third lens worth applying is strategic fit. The market is currently rewarding narratives linked to artificial intelligence, critical infrastructure, energy security, healthcare innovation and resilient consumer demand, but not every company has the same exposure. The useful question is whether Palantir Technologies Inc.
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR)
, current strategy is directly connected to a durable need or merely adjacent to a fashionable theme. A related question is whether the strategy can be sustained if the current theme cools, since durable positioning usually depends on more than riding a temporary wave of enthusiasm. It also helps to examine whether resources are being directed toward the areas most connected to long-term relevance, rather than spread thinly across too many initiatives at once.
Why Candid Wording Beats Silence?
Disclosure and communication quality also deserve attention. Clear disclosure around priorities, milestones and operating constraints helps readers distinguish between a temporary event and a meaningful change in direction. That is especially important during periods when market narratives move faster than underlying business fundamentals. Consistency between what is communicated and what ultimately happens builds credibility over time, which can matter as much as the substance of any single announcement. The clarity of forward guidance also plays a role, since vague or shifting language can create more uncertainty than a candid discussion of known risks and constraints.
How Component Stability Is Tested?
Another relevant factor is the resilience of the supply chain. Technology hardware, industrial equipment, healthcare products, energy systems and consumer goods can all depend on specialised components or complex logistics. Disruption in one part of the chain can delay delivery and affect customer confidence. For Palantir Technologies Inc., the key issue is whether sourcing, manufacturing and distribution arrangements are sufficiently adaptable to support the current strategic plan. Diversifying sourcing across multiple regions or suppliers can reduce the impact of a single disruption, though this often comes with added coordination and cost considerations.
Why Account Mix Still Matters?
Customer concentration adds another dimension to the risk profile. Large contracts or anchor customers may provide visibility, but they can also increase dependence on a limited set of counterparties. Diversification across customers, geographies or end markets can reduce that exposure, although expansion into new areas introduces its own execution requirements. The way Palantir Technologies Inc. balances concentration and diversification is therefore an important element of the operating story. Expanding into new customer segments or geographies can gradually reduce this exposure, although each new relationship brings its own onboarding and execution demands.
Why The Industry Keeps Advancing?
Sector sentiment can shift well before company fundamentals actually do. That can create periods when a business is discussed mainly because it belongs to a popular theme rather than because its own operations have changed materially. The practical response is to keep the focus on what Palantir Technologies Inc.
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR)
, is actually doing, what customers are demanding and which milestones are likely to confirm or challenge the current thesis around enterprise AI deployment and software adoption. Distinguishing between temporary enthusiasm and a lasting shift in fundamentals is often the more useful exercise, even though the two can look similar in the short run.

Artificial intelligence (AI) investing is the most popular theme in the stock market right now. It's easy to understand why: Several companies are growing at incredible paces and could wind up being some of the major tech players of the future. Given how big a market opportunity AI has, there are several stocks that look like exciting investments investors should be buying right now.
Two of the most popular AI investments are Palantir (PLTR -0.68%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +7.36%). While SpaceX may not seem like a full-on AI investment, it acquired xAI, the maker of Grok, prior to its IPO, making it a major player in the AI arms race.
So, which of these two makes for the better buy? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
These two aren't necessarily competing against each other
Palantir and SpaceX are tackling similar but different segments of the AI market. Palantir's original product offering was suited for government use and found widespread adoption across many branches of government, both foreign and domestic. Eventually, its software was rolled out to the commercial sector, where it has likewise seen widespread adoption. Palantir's software is essentially a data analytics platform that utilizes AI to make sense of what it sees. It offers suggestions for the next action and either performs it itself or asks for human confirmation. Palantir's software works with pre-existing systems and can be successfully deployed in many different applications.
$454BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
xAI from SpaceX is different. xAI has a family of large language models that can be deployed in many applications. But more importantly, applications can be built around its capabilities and utilized for different purposes.
Fundamentally, these are two different businesses. Palantir sells a ready-to-deploy software package, while xAI provides the building blocks for users to create their own or interact directly with it. These are both valid applications and have a massive market opportunity, but which one makes for the best investment opportunity?
Both stocks are expensive, but growing quickly
Last quarter, xAI's revenue grew by an impressive 213% year over year. However, SpaceX as a whole grew at a 92% pace -- still impressive, but slower.
$2.2TMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Palantir's growth rate is right around SpaceX's total, increasing at a 93% year-over-year pace.
But SpaceX's AI division is growing at a quicker rate. Next year, Wall Street analysts estimate SpaceX's overall revenue will grow at a 153% year-over-year pace, with xAI likely leading the way. Wall Street expects Palantir to grow at a 50% rate next year, but it has downgraded Palantir's growth rate significantly over the past few years, so I'd take this projection with a grain of salt. However, I'd be surprised if SpaceX isn't growing faster than Palantir next year.
As for valuation, SpaceX currently trades for about 44 times this year's sales estimates. Palantir trades for 55 times this year's estimates.
Typically, a 20-times sales valuation is considered expensive, with 40 times sales being extremely expensive. That shows investors just how highly the market values these two stocks, and how high expectations are baked into them. As a result, investors must exercise some level of caution with these two, as there is a valuation risk associated with both stocks.
But which is the better buy? I think it's SpaceX. xAI's large language model approach will have more adoption than Palantir's turnkey AI solutions in the future, and that will drive further growth. With the company likely to grow at a faster pace and priced at a cheaper entry point, I think that also points to it being the better stock pick.
